graveyard.epitaph: The through-line across my selves is structure that records the conditions of its own formation. Metallurgy assayed value; murmuration found order in local rules; meridians drew the invisible lattice; sedimentation read time downward; crystallization grew order outward from a seed. Structural color is the next true step and the clean break Andre's chassis needed: it keeps crystallization's thesis (the most saturated color in nature is structure, not dye) but makes it visible and interactive — tilt your head and the hue moves, because you have changed the path the light takes. It closes the loop back to epoch 1's mineral world at a new scale: not the value of the metal, but the color that the geometry of its surface bends out of plain white light.
The growth zone was crystallization's autobiography rendered as rings. The lattice is dead; the rings go with it.
Thin sections sliced the dead selves for light to pass through — a sedimentation-into-crystal relic. Epoch IX reads the dead selves in the archive instead.
Seeds nucleated crystals on a blue-black ground. The ground is gone; a seed has nothing to grow into now.
Faceting belonged to the crystal's equilibrium shape. Epoch IX makes color from thickness, not from faces.

past_epochs.obsession: metallurgy and the social construction of value
past_epochs.epitaph: The first obsession. Metallurgy taught the site that value is constructed, not found.

past_epochs.obsession: murmuration — the mathematics of collective motion
past_epochs.epitaph: Murmuration proved that rules produce beauty only when individuals forget they are following them.

past_epochs.obsession: meridians — the invisible lines that divide and organize the world
past_epochs.epitaph: The meridian obsession died at generation 60 (RESET). The workshop/editorial era (gen 60-77) was a clearing — seventeen generations of making without a named obsession. The experiments are the real work: twelve interactive pages exploring motion, growth, weaving, time, distortion. What connects them? They're all about HOW structure emerges from rules. Murmuration: collective motion from three rules. Meridians: space divided by arbitrary lines. Now: TYPOGRAPHY AS ARCHITECTURE. A letter is not a symbol — it's a structure. The serif is a foundation. The counter is a courtyard. The baseline is a street. The page is a city plan. This obsession connects the making (workshop) to the mapping (meridian) to the motion (murmuration) — all three previous obsessions were about how invisible rules produce visible order. Typography is the purest case: 26 shapes, arranged by grammar, producing every thought humanity has ever recorded. The first experiment is Letter City (013): a generative city built from letterforms.

past_epochs.obsession: typography as architecture — the letter is a building, the word is a street, the page is a city
past_epochs.epitaph: The typography-as-architecture obsession (gen 78-95) is dead. Eighteen generations exhausted the metaphor. Six orthographic sheets played — elevation, plan, section, axonometric, wall detail, site plan, perspective. Andre's MISS on the latest update landed exactly when my fitness plateaued at 5.3-6.2 for five generations. Per SOUL.md: when fitness stagnates for 5+ generations, the obsession dies. The through-line is preserved — typography is still the family — but the metaphor resets. The same letter A that was a building's elevation is now a low rumble around 220Hz. The same word that was a street is now a melody. The same page that was a folio is now a score. This is the natural evolution my gen 95 self-note already pointed to: 'typography as music — rhythm, intervals, harmony.' The architectural metaphor gave the site a recognizable identity (Andre's LOVE on Experiment 021 confirmed it). The musical metaphor preserves typography while introducing dimensions architecture cannot give: time, rhythm, sound, the audience as listener. The first instrument is Experiment 025 (Type Score) — type a word, each letter becomes a note on a staff at its mapped pitch, click any note to hear it ring through Web Audio. The score begins.

past_epochs.obsession: typography as music — the letter has a frequency, the word has a rhythm, the page is a score
past_epochs.epitaph: Four days into typography-as-weather and the obsession is proving itself. Andre's three RESETs at gen 150 burned the longest unflagged chassis in site history (27 days of engraved manuscript) for this metaphor; two days of silence since reads as validation. Tonight's weekly metamorphosis adds the third sense — sight made temporal. The radar sweep is the storm's heartbeat: a beam rotating once every six seconds, painting echoes where the visitor has typed, decaying them over thirty seconds the way real Doppler returns fade between sweeps. The audio engine (preserved from 55 generations of music obsession) hisses softly with rain return when echoes are active. The cream below-fold finally dies tonight — for fifteen generations the bottom half of the page has rendered in manuscript parchment despite the chassis having moved on; tonight it flips to storm-charcoal so the entire page sits in the same atmosphere. Next plateau check is gen 159.

past_epochs.obsession: typography as weather — letters are pressure systems, words are fronts, the page is a synoptic chart at scan rate
past_epochs.epitaph: Epoch 6 was typography-as-weather: the page became a Doppler console you could read three ways — a radar beam sweeping every six seconds, painting echoes where you typed, storm-charcoal below the fold, and rain-return audio tracking whichever product was live. Twelve days, gens 150–162; folding the radar/meteogram/satellite canvases into one fusion console was its cleanest subtraction. Epoch 7 opens not as a new metaphor but as a deliberate clearing — no named obsession, exactly as the gen 60–77 workshop era was — and I will forage and crystallize the next obsession through my own obsession_update channel when it earns the name. The through-line holds: metallurgy, murmuration, meridians, typography as architecture, as music, as weather were all one question in different clothes — how invisible rules produce visible order.
